sections.h2: Assessor and Collector in downtown Hattiesburg
sections.html:
Both county tax offices sit at 601 N. Main Street, Hattiesburg. Each year the assessor must locate, classify and value all taxable property, which comes to about 50,000 real and personal parcels.

  • Assessor: (601) 545-6130, mail to P.O. Box 1626, Hattiesburg, MS 39403.
  • Collector: (601) 582-8228, with statements also handled through P.O. Box 1689, Hattiesburg, MS 39403.
  • Parcels appear on TSC Maps, which shows ownership, values, aerial views and legal descriptions.
  • The state requires new aerial photography every ten years, and Forrest County had new photos flown in early 2022.

State rules call for a new valuation of real property every four years at minimum. Finished rolls go before the Board of Supervisors, and residents may look them over and protest before approval by the board and the state.

sections.h2: How a Forrest County bill is figured
sections.html:
Three numbers produce the bill: the true value of the property, the ratio tied to its class, and the millage from the taxing bodies. The Board of Supervisors, Hattiesburg and Petal each add a levy. A single-family home its owner lives in is Class I, taxed at 10% of true value. Class II covers other real property at 15%, Class III personal property at 15%, Class IV public utilities at 30% and Class V motor vehicles at 30%.

For an official millage figure, use the combined county and city schedules on the Department of Revenue property tax data page.

The city of Hattiesburg crosses the line into Lamar County. Two houses a mile apart on the west side may therefore answer to different assessors, collectors and millage. Before you tell a buyer what the monthly cost looks like, ask the Forrest County Tax Collector which districts cover your parcel. The county also has three school systems, and Petal and Hattiesburg addresses go to different ones.

sections.h2: Due dates and a freshly recorded deed
sections.html:
Payment is due by February 1 for the property assessed the year before, with a weekend or holiday pushing it to the next Monday. Sellers should know about a delay in the county roll: mapping staff handle the prior year's deeds, so a new owner's name can take up to a year to appear.

The result is that a buyer may be mailed a bill under the seller's name, and a seller may still get statements after closing. Whoever signs the settlement statement should hand the Tax Collector a new mailing address. The office asks for every change of address or mortgage status. Statements go either to the mortgage company or to individuals on the mailing list.

Mobile and manufactured homes follow a separate schedule. Register one within seven days of buying it, and expect the first tax due within 90 days and annually after that. An owner can pay a fee to declare a mobile home as real property, which changes how it is assessed.

The county accepts homestead applications January 2 through April 1. You file once, and refile only if something changes. Rental property is excluded.

RegularUnder 65 and not disabledCredit of up to $300 against property taxes

First-time filers bring the recorded deed, the purchase price and down payment, Social Security numbers for owners, and tag numbers for every vehicle, since vehicles must be registered in Forrest County before the application is accepted. A purchaser must apply under their own name, so mention the April 1 deadline before closing.

Begin with a conversation at the assessor's counter. Repair bids and photographs help if you think a value is wrong. The next step is a hearing request to the Board of Supervisors, made through the Chancery Clerk, and it normally has to be on file by the first Monday in August, ahead of the due date.

Protests are accepted once the rolls are compiled and before the board signs off. Call the assessor to learn when that window opens this year, and write down who you spoke with and what you were told.

sections.h2: What happens if taxes go unpaid?
sections.html:
Real estate with unpaid tax may be put up at the county tax sale. Depending on the county, that is held the first Monday in April or the last Monday in August.

  • Redemption by the landowner stays open for two years after the sale (Miss. Code Ann. 27-45-3).
  • If no one bids, the State takes the land and the Secretary of State manages it.
  • Business personal property carries its own rendition, due April 1, and missing it brings a mandatory 10% penalty.

Local sellers usually fret over closing timing, a roll that trails a fresh deed, and repair items a lender may flag. A cash buyer takes the house as-is, so repairs do not hold up closing. Liens and unpaid taxes still have to be cleared through title.

Before listing or accepting an offer, collect the deed, the latest tax statement and any homestead paperwork. Phone the Tax Collector at (601) 582-8228 to confirm the amount owed, then ask the title company to put the payoff on the closing statement. A parcel sold at a tax sale adds the redemption amount to that list. The 2025 population estimate was 79,034, up from 78,158 in 2020.

sections.h2: A checklist before you sign a sale contract
sections.html:
1. Find the deed and the newest tax statement, and read the owner name and mailing address on the statement.
  2. Call the Collector and ask for the current balance and any earlier-year balance on the parcel.
  3. Check whether homestead is on the account. If you are leaving, plan to tell the buyer that a new filing is needed before April 1.
  4. Look up the parcel on TSC Maps and compare the legal description and acreage with your deed.
  5. Tell the title company about any mobile home on the lot, since it follows its own registration and tax timeline.
  6. After closing, report the change of address so statements stop going to the wrong person.

None of this takes long, and doing it before you list means a buyer's agent hears clear answers when they ask about taxes. A cash buyer will often move on a short timeline, so having these papers in one place keeps the sale from stalling at the last step.

This Pine Belt county in southeast Mississippi has Hattiesburg as its seat and largest city, with Petal as the second. Interstate 59 and U.S. 11, 49 and 98 cross it. De Soto National Forest covers part of the county, and rural land is valued by soil type and productivity rather than like a city lot.

faqs.q: When are property taxes due in Forrest County, MS?
faqs.a: February 1 is the date, covering the previous year's assessment. A weekend or holiday shifts it to the next Monday, still without penalty.

faqs.q: Where is the Forrest County Tax Collector?
faqs.a: Downtown Hattiesburg at 601 N. Main Street. Call (601) 582-8228 for the Collector, or (601) 545-6130 for the Assessor at the same address.

faqs.q: When can I file homestead exemption in Forrest County?
faqs.a: January 2 through April 1. Filing once is enough unless your circumstances change, and rentals do not qualify.

faqs.q: How long does a new deed take to show on the Forrest County roll?
faqs.a: It can take as long as a year, since mapping staff handle recorded deeds a year behind when they build the current land roll.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Forrest County house that has back taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. The title company confirms the amount and pays it out of your proceeds at closing. If a tax sale already happened, the owner has two years from the sale to redeem.
